haiku-low.q1: Only the SHA-256 hash is stored, in api_tokens. Plaintext appears only in the create response and the user's clipboard, never in the database, logs or analytics.
haiku-low.q2: They cannot. The token is shown once and nobody can show it again, including support and engineering. They must create a new token.
haiku-low.q3: The create request gets 409 with "Limit reached. Revoke a token first." Nothing is stored.
haiku-low.q4: On the next API request. Validity is read from the database on every request with no cache, so revoked_at set means 401.
haiku-low.q5: Each gets a 401 with the same generic body. The responses do not differ, so they do not reveal which case applied.
haiku-low.q6: The server hashes the presented token with SHA-256 and selects the row by hash. It is usable only if not revoked (revoked_at IS NULL) and not expired (expires_at > now()).
haiku-low.q7: A successful API request with an active token triggers it when last_used_at is null or over an hour old. Only that condition causes the write, so it happens at most once an hour per token.
haiku-low.q8: The request still succeeds. The failed last-used write does not affect it; the displayed time is just more out of date.
haiku-low.q9: Revoking sets revoked_at to now() on the row, which is kept. The list query filters on revoked_at IS NULL, so the token disappears from the list.
haiku-low.q10: A token id belonging to another user returns 404, the same answer as for a nonexistent token. The document does not state what happens for an already-revoked token: NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q11: A row exists with its hash, but nobody has the plaintext. The user sees the new name in the list, revokes that token, and creates another.

sonnet.q1: It persists a SHA-256 hash of the token (unique-indexed hash column in api_tokens). The plaintext appears only in the create response (201) and the user's clipboard; never stored in the database, logs or analytics.
sonnet.q2: They can't. Nobody, including support and engineering, can show it again. They must create a new token.
sonnet.q3: The server returns 409 'Limit reached. Revoke a token first.' and nothing is stored.
sonnet.q4: On the very next API request. Validity is not cached, every request reads the database, so it gets 401 with no delay.
sonnet.q5: A 401 with the same generic body in every case (also for missing header). The responses do not differ.
sonnet.q6: It hashes the presented token with SHA-256 and selects the record by that hash. The record is usable only if revoked_at IS NULL and expires_at > now() (i.e. active).
sonnet.q7: A successful API request with an active token where last_used_at is null or older than 1 hour triggers an UPDATE last_used_at = now(). The 'only if null or older than 1 hour' condition limits it to at most one write per token per hour.
sonnet.q8: The request still succeeds. The displayed last-used time is just more out of date.
sonnet.q9: It sets revoked_at = now() on the row (WHERE id and user_id = session user); the row is not deleted. The list query filters revoked_at IS NULL, so the revoked token no longer appears in the list.
sonnet.q10: Another user's token id gives 404 (same answer as no such token). Already-revoked token: NOT STATED.
sonnet.q11: The row exists in the database but nobody has the plaintext, and the server cannot re-send it since it never stored it. The user sees the new name in the list, revokes it, and creates another.
